article.title: Meta acquires AI coding startup Conductor | TechCrunch
article.text:
Meta has acquired Conductor, an AI coding startup that allows users to spin up software projects by deploying multiple agents into parallel workspaces.
The news was originally reported by Axios, and Conductor shared news of its acquisition on its blog.
“I have big news: Conductor is joining Meta,” wrote the startup’s founder and CEO, Charlie Holtz, on Wednesday. “We have some big, crazy plans for the next interface,” he added, teasing that the company would have “something new” for customers to use by “early next year.”
On X, Holtz also noted that he was looking forward to working with Alexandr Wang, Meta’s chief AI officer, and Nat Friedman, head of product at the company’s Superintelligence Labs. “They’ve been on an absolute tear, and I’m convinced MSL has the highest talent density of all the labs,” he added.
Meta confirmed the acquisition to TechCrunch but wouldn’t comment further or provide additional details about the deal.
Conductor, founded in 2024, only launched its core product just last summer. The company’s agentic teams, which can be deployed in the cloud, locally, or via a user’s phone, are designed to help software engineers work on separate, compartmentalized parts of a project in concert. The agents that the platform deploys aren’t developed in-house but come from major labs like Anthropic and OpenAI.
Holtz said that, until early next year, Conductor’s core features would continue to work as they previously have. The exception is Conductor’s cloud service, which will shut down on November 20, after which the company will begin deleting user cloud data.
Meta, which previously lagged behind in AI services, has spent the last several months trying to catch up. In August, the company launched Muse Code, its own coding agent. Meanwhile, the company’s recently launched Muse agents are seeing significant adoption, with the company recently reporting that the service had surpassed 10 million users. The company has also made a number of AI-related acquisitions over the past year, including Moltbook, the viral agent platform that made headlines.

article.title: Introducing SWE-2 Flash | Cognition
article.text:
Introducing SWE-2 Flash
By The Cognition Team2026.11.04
We’re introducing SWE-2 Flash, a fully American coding model that sets a new bar for intelligence at low cost and high speed. For the first time, we added a mid-training stage before reinforcement learning in our recipe. This results in significant gains over the base model, Inkling-Small from Thinking Machines, improving Terminal-Bench 4.0 from 0.9% to 20.0% and FrontierCode 2.0 from 3.2% to 24.0%.
On leading evals, SWE-2 Flash outperforms all American open-weight models, even models that are 3x larger. To balance transparent access and cyber risks, we are building a program to securely share the weights with industry partners and researchers.

As model capabilities continue to advance, we remain focused on lowering the cost of everyday engineering work in addition to pushing the capabilities frontier. Today, smaller models are increasingly able to handle a significant portion of the work that software agents do, such as automations, code review, feature development, and updating documentation.
We developed SWE-2 Flash to satisfy this growing need. It is available today in Devin Desktop and CLI, at one-fifth the price and 3x the speed of its much larger sibling, SWE-2.

Training#
We began with a large-scale mid-training stage on top of Inkling-Small, a model with 276B total and 12B active parameters. A key challenge was determining the right data mix: which sources to include, and in what proportions. To guide these decisions, we curated a high-quality held-out coding dataset that reflects model intelligence in real-world software engineering scenarios.
We then used token efficiency plots to evaluate different data sources and identify the most effective mixtures. Starting with a baseline training run, we measured how many tokens each candidate data mix needed to reach the same validation loss as the baseline. By plotting the ratio of these token counts on the y-axis and baseline tokens on the x-axis, we could directly compare the training efficiency of different mixtures.
Token efficiency of each data mix
We iterated on the composition of our mid-training data and converged on a dataset composed of a few trillion tokens of high-quality scientific articles, blogs, code, and other sources. Training proceeded in three stages, so that the model would see the scarcest, highest-quality data later in training. Throughout each stage, held-out validation loss improved at a stable log-linear rate.
Validation loss across mid-training
We followed the mid-training phase with large-scale reinforcement learning. While we made some tweaks to our RL recipe from SWE-2, most of the improvements came from the much higher quality and diversity of our RL tasks.
On quality, we carefully audited the instructions, environment setup, and verifiers for our tasks. On diversity, we curated several new task types covering a far wider range of capabilities than before, to build the general reasoning and problem-solving skills that real…

article.title: Recursive Self-Improvement via AI for Chip Design & Chip Design for AI - Ricursive Intelligence
article.text:
Introducing Ripple-65B Preview,
a Frontier Open-Weight Model
Achieving U.S. Open-Weight SOTA on Agentic Coding
Achieving U.S. Open-Weight SOTA on Agentic Coding
Ricursive Intelligence is a full-stack artificial intelligence lab building self-improving systems by co-optimizing hardware, software, and model.
To power our chip design platform, we trained a language model from scratch that sets a new U.S. open-weight SOTA on agentic coding. We optimized the model architecture for our training and serving platforms, driving substantial efficiency gains.
Today, we release Ripple-65B Preview, a general-purpose variant of the proprietary model that powers our AI chip design platform. The model is pretrained on 12 trillion tokens with support for up to 1M context length. Ripple-65B Preview delivers strong results on agentic coding, achieving U.S. open-weight state-of-the-art (80.52) on TerminalBench 2.1 and surpassing significantly larger US open-weight models such as Reflection Beam 501B (80.1), Meta Muse Spark Open 816B (76.4), Thinking Machines Inkling 975B (63.8), and NVIDIA Nemotron 3 Ultra 550B (56.4).
Ripple’s dense model architecture provides strong reasoning performance with low-latency token generation. The model’s small parameter envelope also enables it to run efficiently on local devices such as NVIDIA DGX Spark, which feature high compute FLOPs with low memory bandwidth relative to datacenter accelerators.
Ripple-65B Preview is available on Hugging Face, Together AI, GMI Cloud, and OpenRouter. Fireworks goes live later today.
Achieving U.S. Open-Weight Frontier at One-Tenth Cost
LLM pretraining is legendarily expensive. In 2023, OpenAI CEO Sam Altman said that GPT-4 training costs exceeded $100 million. In the following year, Dario Amodei said that frontier AI models can cost up to $1 billion to train, projecting that costs would rise to $10-100B by 2026 to 2027 for pretraining alone.
In contrast, we developed and trained Ripple-65B Preview for only $32M, which is one-tenth the cost of the previous open-weight SOTA on agentic coding, as estimated to the best of our knowledge.¹ Note that $32M is our full R&D cost starting from scratch, including pretraining ladder development, data mixing, evals, debugging, synthetic data generation, posttraining recipe development, and the final hero pretraining and posttraining run.
Steep Ascent Reinforcement Learning
Rather than investing in a brute-force RL climb, we carefully iterated on our SFT and RL recipes with a focus on compute efficiency. We opted not to buy any posttraining data, instead devising our own synthetic data pipelines, quality filtering, and coverage metrics.
Our mixed RL recipe uses truncated importance sampling, score centering, and linear length penalty with high-quality long-horizon synthetic environments. The RL tasks are tuned for our model capabilities, and we continuously added harder tasks as the model improved.
The end result was a steep RL climb from a strong initial SFT checkpoint. We reached a TerminalBench 2.1 score of 80.5 with only 1.4M rollouts, roughly 70x fewer rollouts than Reflection Beam, the prior SOTA.
A Co-Designed Model Architecture
Ripple-65B Preview’s architecture was designed to be trained and served efficiently on NVIDIA hardware. A key objective was to make design decisions which reduce pretraining and posttraining infrastructure complexity while still enabling strong reasoning and agentic performance. Therefore, we chose to train a modernized dense Transformer model rather than use Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) like other labs. This decision quickly paid off, and we were able to train a strong model from scratch while maintaining a solid MFU (40%) throughout pretraining and posttraining, even with simple sharding, no custom kernels, and no quantization.
Ripple-65B Preview uses a thin-and-deep model aspect ratio, with a narrow d_model (5120) and 80 total layers. To improve reasoning performance, we overprovision the number of attention…

article.title: Changelog | Google Antigravity Docs
article.text:
v2.29.0
Latest
November 3, 2026
Jupyter notebook viewer, redesigned Automations, voice mode, and remote agents
This release adds a native Jupyter notebook viewer, redesigned Home and Automations pages, and downloads and browsing history in the built-in browser. Voice mode, powered by Gemini Live, and remote agents, which run conversations in the cloud, are starting to roll out.
Improvements(22)
Jupyter notebook .ipynb files now open natively in the file viewer, rendering code cells, Markdown, tables, images, and cell outputs without leaving Antigravity.
Voice mode, powered by Gemini Live, lets you talk to Antigravity and hand requests to the agent by voice. Start it from the button in an empty message box. Voice mode is rolling out gradually, so you may not see it yet.
Remote agents are starting to roll out to Google AI Ultra and Pro subscribers. Conversations in a cloud project run in the cloud instead of on your computer, and you can also open them at antigravity.google.com/remote.
The new-conversation page now greets you at the top and pins the message box to the bottom. Single-repo projects combine branch and Git worktree selection into one menu, and the agent picker now lives inside the model menu.
The Automations page now organizes automations into Scheduled, Always on, and Paused lists with Next run and Last run times, plain-menu schedule pickers, in-page details, and a full-page creation form.
Long conversations in the conversation navigator now label each collapsed chapter card with a short AI-generated title instead of only a date.
The built-in browser now saves downloads directly to your downloads folder without blocking prompts, shows progress in a toolbar downloads drawer, and lets you choose a default download folder under Settings > General.
Typing in the built-in browser's address bar now suggests matching pages from your browsing history, and you can clear saved history under Settings > General.
The built-in browser has a redesigned address bar with clearer connection security indicators, a thin loading progress bar along the top of the page, and an in-page prompt dialog when a site asks for text input.
You can now open a web address or search Google from the side panel's New Tab page, drag links into the side panel to open them in the built-in browser, and close tabs to the left from a tab's menu.
Settings > Appearance now includes a Fill option that expands conversations to the full width of the center pane, a Font menu to switch between System UI, Inter, and Google Sans, and a Screen Reader Mode toggle under Accessibility.
If you haven't picked your own, Antigravity now uses the Onyx theme and the Google Sans font. You can change both under Settings > Appearance.
You can now customize keyboard shortcuts in Settings > Shortcuts, and reset any of them to the default.
Code blocks and diffs now load syntax highlighting on demand across 173 languages, and the file tree and tabs include file icons for more than 30 additional languages and config formats.
The Overview panel's Review row and the Review tab header now show total added and deleted line counts across changed files in your Git repository.
Opening antigravity:// links can now jump directly to a plugin or skill in the Marketplace, or open a new conversation with the prompt filled in for you to review and send.
The Git branch menu now adds a search box when a repository has more than 15 branches, refreshes automatically when you return to the window, and shows the checked-out commit hash when in detached HEAD state.
Agent question cards can now be collapsed while you read earlier messages and are automatically canceled if you send a new reply instead, and each permission preset in the message box now has its own icon.
In conversation search, you can now unarchive an archived conversation directly from its row, and the Automations filter includes archived automation runs.

article.title: Changelog - Kiro
article.text:
Share credits across your team with credit pooling
Loading image...
Enterprise administrators can now share Kiro credits across seated users with credit pooling. In the Kiro console, the feature is labeled Credit sharing. Each seat costs $20 per month and adds 500 monthly credits to one shared pool, so credits one user doesn't use stay available to the rest of the team. Seat price and credits are prorated for the first month.
Admins can add users or groups, set per-user, per-group, and per-profile usage limits, monitor pool usage, and buy additional credits that are good for one year from purchase. Credit pooling is the only option for new Kiro profiles. Existing customers can move users from individual subscriptions with the Switch to credit sharing wizard. You can't undo the switch. Learn more ->
V3 by Default, Classic and Desktop App Retired
This release makes V3 the default agent harness for interactive Kiro CLI sessions on hosts that can run it. Existing V2 users are asked before the default applies, and Kiro upgrades custom agents still in the V2 format unless you turn that off. Kiro CLI is now a single standalone kiro-cli binary that retires the Classic interface, the desktop app, and inline autocomplete.
V3 brings capabilities V2 does not have. Cloud sessions let you disconnect and resume later from /sessions. Memory, once enabled, carries repository context forward. Approve for me, once enabled, approves routine actions, blocks unsafe ones, and asks about the rest while your deny, ask, and allow rules still decide first. /sandbox isolates shell commands, /autonomous on runs tasks without per-command approval with sandboxing on, and Workflows show their plan before starting. Turn on Workflows under /settings > Features.
Breaking changes
Classic interface: The Classic (V1) interactive experience no longer runs. If your command, alias, or settings still select it, Kiro offers Continue with V3 when you start a chat, and scripts ignore the selection. To keep the V2 agent, run kiro-cli --v2. Learn more ->
Desktop app: Kiro CLI no longer ships the desktop app. Existing macOS desktop app installs switch to the standalone kiro-cli on their next update check. To reinstall or change how Kiro CLI is installed, see Moving from the Kiro CLI desktop app.
Autocomplete and inline suggestions: Inline shell autocomplete and inline suggestions are retired with the desktop app and have no standalone replacement. The autocomplete, inline, translate, theme, and dashboard commands are unavailable; remove them from your scripts. Running kiro-cli doctor now directs you to kiro-cli diagnostic or kiro-cli issue.
Start on V3 by default
V3 is now the default. You no longer need --v3.
Interactive: New sessions start on V3. If you already use V2, you'll be asked first.
Headless: By default, scripts using --trust-all-tools start on V3. Other scripts stay on V2.
ACP: By default, new clients start on V3. Existing clients stay on V2 unless already supported.
Learn more ->
Generally Available: Claude Opus 5.5, GPT-5.6 Sol
Claude Opus 5.5 and GPT-5.6 Sol are generally available with full Kiro support. Expanded capacity supports more dependable access for production workloads. Their current plans, regions, surfaces, context windows, credit multipliers, and inference scopes remain unchanged.
Both models' Experimental labels no longer apply. The Kiro Excluded Models indemnity exception also no longer applies to these models. To load the latest model list, restart the IDE or CLI, run kirocrew restart for Crew, or refresh Web in your browser. Learn more ->
Automatic V2 Agent Upgrades and ACP Sign-In
This release turns on automatic V2 agent upgrades by default when a V3 session starts and lets ACP clients that declare terminal authentication sign in to Kiro from a terminal. Custom agents built for V2 keep working on V3 without a manual upgrade run, and a capable client opens a terminal sign-in flow. It also draws Mermaid node shapes and nested subgraphs, adds…

This decision quickly paid off, and we were able to train a strong model from scratch while maintaining a solid MFU (40%) throughout pretraining and posttraining, even with simple sharding, no custom kernels, and no quantization.
Ripple-65B Preview uses a thin-and-deep model aspect ratio, with a narrow d_model (5120) and 80 total layers. To improve reasoning performance, we overprovision the number of attention…

article.title: Changelog | Kimi Code Docs
article.text:
Changelog ​
This page documents the changes in each Kimi Code CLI release.
2.5.0 (2026-11-04) ​
Features ​
Use /model and /effort while the Agent is working. A turn that has already started calling the model keeps its settings, the switch applies from the next turn, and choosing Compact and continue runs after the current turn ends.
Fork a session from a selected historical turn or while it is still running.
Merge Skills from every configured directory in multi-directory projects, with the primary directory taking precedence on name conflicts.
Add creation-time SSH, Docker, and custom-command environments. Use --environment <id> to select an environment and optionally --environment-cwd <path> to set its working directory.
Polish ​
Speed up remote file reads, edits, writes, search, and completion.
Improve plugin marketplace interactions.
Show steered messages faded until the Agent reads them, including across turns.
Show backend model error messages verbatim, stop inferring quota from message wording, and require explicit retryability for retry policies.
Stop requiring Edit and prohibiting Bash sed for incremental file edits.
Refresh available tools during the current turn after MCP authentication or other tool changes.
Show background task notifications while their resulting turn is running.
Keep long-running subagent cards responsive as streamed output grows.
Remind the Agent to update its todo list after 10 steps without an update instead of 5, and do not remind it while the list still matches its progress.
Show the remote working directory in the welcome panel and the remote repository's Git status in the footer when using a remote environment. Update Web and Desktop PR badges immediately after switching branches, never run a git or gh executable located inside the opened folder when reading Git status, and remove the leftover “Ready.” line after startup.
Set [workspace] require_trust = false to skip workspace trust prompts.
Web: improved interactions and fixed known bugs.
Bug Fixes ​
Fix sessions sometimes still appearing in session lists right after being archived.
Record each custom-registry model's advertised output token limit to fix 400 Invalid max_tokens errors.
Fix ACP initialization failing when clients send the first request during startup.
Fix searches failing on dot-only filenames, completion exceeding its timeout, and false directory warnings.
Fix local file tools in existing Desktop sessions after upgrading.
Fix cancelling one MCP sign-in attempt interrupting another.
Fix model refresh reporting custom-registry providers as updated when nothing changed.
Fix the first side-chat answer sometimes showing the main conversation's answer or disappearing, and fix side-chat history dropping or reordering earlier turns after the server reloads a session from disk.
Show the invalid workspace directory path instead of silently exiting during TUI startup.
Fix the todo list not reverting after undo.
Fix @ file mentions to include files from additional workspace directories.
Other ​
Add Server WebSocket agent, usage, goal, todo, task.list, and task frames for Agent state, settings, context usage, goals, todos, and task changes. Transcripts and REST transcript endpoints no longer include meta, todos, or tasks; remove GET /sessions/{id}/status and the status field of the :undo response.
Remove WebSocket subscribe / unsubscribe, cursor replay, resync_required, GET /sessions/{id}/snapshot, and the session last_seq field. Use subscribe_v2 and send it again after reconnecting. event.session.work_changed now reaches every connection for every live session.
Remove the REST task endpoints and their :cancel / :detach actions. Use WebSocket task.watch / task.unwatch to stream output and task.stop / task.background to stop a task or move it to the background.
Stop building the global full-text search index by default. POST /api/v1/search reports the index as unavailable and past sessions are no longer scanned in the background; set…
